query: Consider the following context: Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. In that context, which material can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy system with a specific composition and processing conditions can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
generation.intervention: high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment or specific processing conditions
generation.structural_mediator: microstructure with coherent interfaces or specific phase composition
generation.mechanism: The HPHT-induced hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces allows dislocations to transfer between phases, relieving stress concentration and preventing interfacial cracking. This coherency facilitates the progressive activation of multiple deformation mechanisms (dislocations, stacking faults, microbands, and twins) at multiple length scales, leading to strain delocalization and enhanced work hardening. Derived from materials-science principles and partially transferring records.
generation.uncertainty: limited understanding of the underlying mechanisms and complexity of the alloy composition

Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s). Findings: The addition of 4.2 at% Cr led to the formation of a Laves phase in addition to the BCC phase, whereas the base alloy was single-phase BCC.; The hardness of HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 reached 535.8 Hv0.3, which is 56.96% higher than the reference alloy HfMoTaTiZr (460.1 Hv0.3).; The yield strength of HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 reached 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa, which is 207.5 MPa higher than HfMoTaTi

Paper card. Question: Can high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in eutectic high entropy alloys (EHEAs) that are typically strong yet brittle?. System: Al0.7CoCrFeNi (Al 14.8 Co 21.3 Cr 21.3 Fe 21.3 Ni 21.3 at. %). Processing: Homogenized alloy subjected to HPHT treatment at 6 GPa and 1473 K for 2 hours using a self-designed hexahedron-anvil-press apparatus. Test conditions: Uniaxial quasi-static tensile tests at room temperature with a strain rate of 3 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. Findings: The HPHT-treated alloy achieved a tensile strength of 1150 MPa and a tensile ductility of 36%, representing a doubling of both properties compared to the precursor.; The HPHT-treated alloy exhibited a true fracture stress of ~1570 MPa, significantly higher than the as-cast, as-cast+HPHT, and homogenized alloys.; The HPHT-treated alloy showed a uniform tensile elongation of ~36%, whereas the homogenized (Ho) alloy only exhibited ~14.7%.; The HPHT treatment induced a hierarchically patterned microstructure with hexagonal-like structural units interconnected by the FCC phase.; The mismatch factor between the FCC and B2 phases in the HPHT-treated alloy was cal

Question: What are the elastic and plastic deformation behaviors of the NbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy at room temperature and elevated temperatures, and how do they compare to conventional BCC alloys?. System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25) BCC refractory high-entropy alloy. Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere from 99.99 wt% purity elements, melted 10 times, drop-cast into 4-mm diameter rods, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, followed by water cooling. Test conditions: In situ neutron diffraction and compressive testing at room temperature (RT), 500°C, 700°C, and 900°C with a strain rate of 1 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; Resonant Ultrasound Spectroscopy (RUS) at RT; First-principles calculations at -273°C and RT. Paper card. Question: How can the room temperature ductility of an initially brittle refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with a continuous ordered B2 matrix be improved while maintaining high yield strength?. System: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr (RHEA). Processing: Condition (1): Cast, hot isostatically pressed (HIPed) at 1200 °C for 2 h, homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, slow cooled at 10 °C/min. Condition (2): Condition (1) solutionized at 1400 °C for 20 min, water quenched. Condition (3): Condition (2) annealed at 600 °C for 120 hrs, water quenched.. Test conditions: Room temperature (25 °C) and elevated temperature (600 °C) uniaxial compression tests at an initial strain rate of 0.001 s⁻¹.. Findings: Condition (1) exhibited a continuous ordered B2 matrix with discrete BCC precipitates, resulting in a yield strength of 2032 MPa but only 4.7% compressive fracture strain.; Condition (2) formed a single-phase weakly ordered BCC structure with nanometer-scale B2 regions, achieving >60% compressive ductility but a lower yield strength of 1065 MPa.; Condition (3) achieved an 'inverted' microstructure with a continuous disordered BCC matrix and discrete ~50 nm B2 precipitates, yielding 1345

Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
